newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries close lower, await five-year sale.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries close lower, await five-year sale.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries closed lower in thin trading on Wednesday as investors took profits and adjusted positions ahead of an auction of five-year Treasury notes scheduled for Thursday, analysts said.
The 6-1/2-percent 30-year benchmark Treasury bond ended off 19/32 at 95-24/32. Its yield rose to 6.83 percent against 6.79 percent on Tuesday.
"You'll have five-year notes to underwrite tomorrow and the market is giving up some ground here ahead of that," said John Spinello, a managing director at Merrill Lynch.
The market grew wary of upcoming supply as underwriters for the $12.5 billion 5-year note sale appeared to be scarce despite solid demand at the two-year note sale on Wednesday.
"I don't think the five-year will be as easy to underwrite as the two-year note was and I think that there are duration problems with it ... there is more risk," Spinello said.

Some experts said, however, some bidders are likely to show up if the five-year note yield rises to somewhere around 6.35 percent. "I don't know if it's going to happen, but I know there will be people interested in buying it at those levels," said a trader at a U.S. investment bank.
In late when-issued trading on Wednesday, the five-year note was yielding 6.3275 percent.
The two-year notes were placed with a yield of 5.984 percent, below market expectations of 6.0 percent. The sale's bid-to-cover ratio was 2.44, considered by several players to be "fairly high."

The market's knee-jerk reaction to the auction results was positive, but no heavy flows followed and prices quickly slipped back into the red column. "There was not a lot of subsequent flows to the results," Spinello said.
Despite the sharp drop in prices on Wednesday, some experts said trading was technical and the market was mostly rangebound.

"The market came down and retraced about half of yesterday's range (when the benchmark bond rose more than half a point)," said Matthew Alexy, chief fixed-income market strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston.
"So a big part of this is simply range trade more than anything else," he added. Alexy sees the bellwether 30-year bond yield ranging primarily between 6.76 percent and 6.86 percent.
"(But) there is a big yield channel. If we get uglier news and we begin to break out ... Then you can go about 10 basis points higher to 6.96 percent," Alexy added.

Alexy acknowledged the heavy upcoming supply might be a drag on the market, but he added he did not expect the auctions would propel rates much higher. "I don't think the supply will cause the market to break to new high yield levels but it will certainly contain the market," he said.
The Treasury will offer the market some $60 billion in new securities over the next few weeks, including the first $7.0 billion in inflation-indexed 10-year notes.
The three-month Treasury bill rate closed flat at 5.03 percent. The six-month bill rate rose one basis point to 5.11 percent. The year bill rate was up two points at 5.29 percent.

The two-year note closed down 2/32 at 99-18/32, yielding 5.99 percent. The five-year note traded off 5/32 at 99-5/32 to yield 6.33 percent. The ten-year note closed down 10/32 at 99-19/32, yielding 6.56 percent.
The market mostly shrugged off the release of the Federal Reserve's Beige Book, analysts said.
The survey said the U.S. economy was growing at a moderate pace. The Fed also detected some signs of wage pressures, but no big price pressures apart from energy.
Market participants also learned that December housing starts dropped 12.2 percent to a 1.329 million annual rate against a 9.3 percent rise in the previous month.
The data had little impact on prices.
Flows were mixed. "We didn't see any major player or group of players standing out in the market today," one trader said.
